title: What You'll Build - DBANK (Inspired by Compound)
section: 38. Build Your First Defi (Decentralised Finance) DApp - DBANK
summary: Short project intro for the DBANK DeFi app: a simplified money-market idea in which a token balance earns interest, written in Motoko for the Internet Computer. Also positions Motoko as a general-purpose language that feels familiar to JS/TS/Swift/Java/C# developers.

concepts.heading: The inspiration: money-market protocols
points: Compound is a money-market protocol: holders supply tokens (e.g. Ether) to earn interest, and borrowers take out tokens such as Chainlink and repay later.
Borrowers pay interest; the protocol passes it to lenders and keeps a small fee for running the service.
DBANK is a cut-down version: no borrowing side, just one account whose balance grows with interest over time.

concepts.heading: What the project will cover
points: A Motoko backend (canister) that stores a balance, accepts top-ups and withdrawals, and compounds interest based on elapsed time.
A JavaScript/HTML/CSS frontend that talks to that backend (built in later lessons of this section).
Final goal for the backend: earn interest on a token balance, implemented purely in Motoko.

concepts.heading: About Motoko
points: Motoko comes from DFINITY, with Andreas Rossberg (a WebAssembly co-creator) as lead designer.
It is designed as a modern general-purpose language, aimed specifically at writing Internet Computer smart contracts (canisters).
Syntax resembles JavaScript, TypeScript, Swift, C# and Java, so prior experience transfers quickly.
(Extra) Motoko compiles to WebAssembly, which is what canisters run as on the Internet Computer.

playground.coverage: No playground lesson yet (the playground has no files for section 38).
gaps_and_ideas: Proposed lesson 'DBANK intro: compound interest in a canister'. Blurb: preview of the finished DBANK page and the idea that a balance grows over time.

Tasks: (1) read the finished UI screenshot and list the three actions (top up, withdraw, check balance); (2) write the compound formula balance * 1.01^seconds in plain JS; (3) predict the balance after 60 s on 300; (4) list which pieces live in the backend vs frontend.
Interactive demo idea: a slider for elapsed seconds that shows the compounded balance from a 300 starting value, to preview what the Motoko code later computes.
